Given: ore analysis (mass %): 5.65 Cu, 20 Fe, 6.2 Zn, 25.9 S, 23.3 \mathrm{SiO_2}, 10.2 \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, 4.0 CaO, 1.0 BaO, 3.1 \mathrm{CO_2}, 0.7 \mathrm{H_2O}. Minerals present: chalcopyrite \mathrm{CuFeS_2}, pyrite \mathrm{FeS_2}, sphalerite ZnS. Atomic masses Cu 63.55, Fe 55.85, Zn 65.38, S 32.06.

Find: the mineralogical (phase) composition of the ore.

Basis and logic: 100 g of ore. Cu occurs only in chalcopyrite and Zn only in sphalerite; the Fe left after chalcopyrite is in pyrite; sulphur is then used as a check. The other components are reported as analysed, since no other minerals were identified.

Step 1, gram-atoms in 100 g.

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Cu} &= 5.65/63.55 = 0.0889 & \mathrm{Fe} &= 20/55.85 = 0.3581 \\ \mathrm{Zn} &= 6.2/65.38 = 0.0948 & \mathrm{S} &= 25.9/32.06 = 0.8079 \end{aligned}

Step 2, chalcopyrite. One Cu gives one \mathrm{CuFeS_2}: 0.0889 mol, which takes 0.0889 g-atom Fe and 2 \times 0.0889 = 0.1778 g-atom S.

Step 3, pyrite. Fe left = 0.3581 - 0.0889 = 0.2692 g-atom, so \mathrm{FeS_2} = 0.2692 mol, which takes 2 \times 0.2692 = 0.5384 g-atom S.

Step 4, sphalerite. ZnS = 0.0948 mol, which takes 0.0948 g-atom S.

Step 5, sulphur check. S needed = 0.1778 + 0.5384 + 0.0948 = 0.8110 g-atom = 26.0 g, against 25.9 g analysed. The 0.1 g gap is within analytical rounding, so the three minerals account for all the S.

Step 6, masses. With M = 183.52 (\mathrm{CuFeS_2}), 119.97 (\mathrm{FeS_2}) and 97.44 (ZnS) \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}:

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{CuFeS_2} &= 0.0889 \times 183.52 = 16.3\ \mathrm{g} \\ \mathrm{FeS_2} &= 0.2692 \times 119.97 = 32.3\ \mathrm{g} \\ \mathrm{ZnS} &= 0.0948 \times 97.44 = 9.2\ \mathrm{g} \end{aligned}

1b.html:
Definition. Ore dressing is the physical (and sometimes limited chemical) treatment of an ore that separates the value minerals from the gangue, giving a concentrate and tailings that can be treated economically for metal extraction. It produces no metal.

Importance.

  • Less tonnage to ship and to heat, flux or leach, so freight and extraction cost fall.
  • Less slag, so less metal lost in it.
  • Lean ores become workable (0.5% Cu rock is processed today), which expands reserves.
  • Complex Cu-Pb-Zn ores give separate concentrates (selective beneficiation).

Steps.

  1. Comminution: crushing (jaw, gyratory, cone crushers) and grinding (rod and ball mills) until the particle size approaches the grain size, so the value mineral is liberated; over-grinding is avoided.
  2. Sizing: screening for coarse sizes, classification by settling velocity for fine sizes; oversize returns to the mill.
  3. Concentration (particle selection): by specific gravity (jigs, tables, heavy media), magnetism, electrical conductivity or surface wettability (froth flotation), giving concentrate, middlings and tailings.
  4. Dewatering: thickening, filtration and drying of the concentrate.
pts: Defines ore dressing as separation of value minerals from gangue, mainly by physical methods, giving a concentrate and tailings without producing metal
Lists at least three points of importance: lower freight and extraction cost, less metal lost in slag, lean ores workable (0.5% Cu), separate concentrates from complex ores
Comminution: crushing and grinding to liberate the value mineral, without over-grinding
Sizing: screening and classification, oversize returned to the mill
Concentration methods matched to the property used (density, magnetism, conductivity, wettability), with concentrate, middlings and tailings
Dewatering: thickening, filtration and drying

1c.html:
Commercial size reduction applies stress in three ways, and each gives a different product size:

  1. Slow compression (jaw, gyratory and smooth roll crushers). Stress is set up throughout the particle and raised gradually until the resolved tensile and shear stresses are just enough to propagate the pre-existing cracks. The largest cracks run first, so fracture occurs at only a few places: a few large fragments, relatively large compared with the original particle, in a narrow size range.
  2. Fast compression or impact (hammer, stamp, impact at the toe of a ball mill). The rapid loading extends the existing cracks and forms new ones, so the particle shatters into many fragments much smaller than the original, over a wide size range.
  3. Abrasion (rubbing against neighbouring particles or hard surfaces, as in zones A and B of a tumbling mill). High shear stresses act only near the surface, so fracture is localised at the surface. The distribution is bimodal: one mode close to the original size (the worn core) and one at very small sizes (the fines).

So the faster and more localised the stress, the finer the product: crushers working by slow compression make coarse products, mills working by impact and abrasion make fines.
pts: Names the three techniques: slow compression, fast compression (impact) and abrasion
Slow compression: stress raised gradually until pre-existing (largest) cracks propagate, fracture at a few places, so a few large fragments close to the original size
Fast compression: existing cracks extended and new cracks formed, so many fragments much smaller than the original over a wide range
Abrasion: high shear near the surface, fracture localised at the surface, so a bimodal distribution (one mode near the original size, one very fine)
Sketch of the fragments or the size distributions for the three techniques
Links each technique to machines (crushers by slow compression, impact in hammer or ball mills, abrasion in tumbling mills) and concludes which gives the finest product

2b.html:
A ball mill is a horizontal cylinder, 30 to 50% filled with hard steel or ceramic balls and the ore (usually with water), rotating about its axis. The balls are free to move, and the size reduction comes from the motion of this charge.

Lifting. As the shell rotates, friction and the liner lift the charge up the rising side. At the shoulder, centrifugal action no longer balances the weight. The charge then falls under gravity, rolling down the surface (cascading) or thrown clear in free flight (cataracting), and lands at the toe.

Zones (see sketch).

  1. Zone A (against the rising shell): most of the charge is lifted with the lining, but some moves in the opposite direction (shearing). Size reduction by abrasion and impact.
  2. Zone B (the sloping surface): particles move with their neighbours, in intimate contact, tumbling over each other. Abrasion and impact; this is the major grinding zone.
  3. Free fall: no contact between particles, so no size reduction until they land.
  4. Zone C, the impact zone (toe): size reduction solely by impact of particles that fell from the opposite side. The fall must land on the charge, not on the bare liner, or liner wear rises sharply.

Speed. The critical speed holds a particle on the shell for a full turn, Mg = 2Mv^2/D with v = \pi D N/60:

N_c = \frac{42.3}{\sqrt{D}}\ \mathrm{rpm}\quad (D\ \text{in m})

Too slow, the balls only roll down (cascading) and grinding is limited; too fast, the charge sticks to the shell (centrifuging) and there is hardly any grinding. Mills run at 65 to 82% of N_c: for D = 2 m, N_c = 29.9 rpm and the mill runs at about 19 to 25 rpm.

Liners and filling. Profiled (lifter) liners lift the charge higher at a given speed; they reduce shearing but increase the action in zone B. The filling (30 to 50%) sets the share of the charge in each zone, so it controls the breakage mechanism and the grinding rate.
pts: Neat sketch: shell with direction of rotation, charge lifted to the shoulder, free-fall paths onto the toe, zones A, B and C and the no-grinding region labelled
Charge lifted up the rising side by the lining until, at the shoulder, centrifugal action no longer balances the weight and it falls under gravity
Zone A: most of the charge lifted with the lining, some opposite movement (shearing); size reduction by abrasion and impact
Zone B: particles in intimate contact tumbling over each other; abrasion and impact; the major grinding zone
Free fall: no contact between particles, so no size reduction until the impact zone
Zone C (toe): size reduction solely by impact; falling charge should strike the charge, not the liner, to limit liner wear
Critical speed N_c = 42.3/\sqrt{D} rpm; too slow gives cascading (little grinding), too fast gives centrifuging (no grinding); runs at 65 to 82% of N_c
Profiled (lifter) liners raise the lift at a given speed, reduce shearing and increase action in zone B
Filling of 30 to 50% sets the proportion of charge in each zone, hence the breakage mechanism and rate

2c.html:
Closed circuit grinding is running a mill (usually a ball mill) with a classifier or screen that splits the discharge into the finished product and the oversize, which returns to the mill as the circulating load (commonly 200 to 1000% of the new feed).

Why. A ball mill also grinds particles already fine enough, so batch grinding to, say, all minus 65 mesh over-grinds much of the ore (hard to concentrate, energy wasted), while a short open-circuit pass leaves oversize. In closed circuit the ore passes quickly with little over-grinding (sliming), and the classifier keeps the oversize in the circuit.
pts: Defines it: the mill works with a classifier or screen that takes the discharge and returns the oversize to the mill
Names the returned stream the circulating load (about 200 to 1000% of the new feed)
Reason: batch or long grinding over-grinds (sliming, energy waste), and open circuit leaves oversize
Result: rapid passage through the mill with little over-grinding and a product of the required size

3a.html:
Given: head F = 2000 g at f = 2.1\% Pb; concentrate C = 70 g at c = 55.1\% Pb; tailing assay t = 0.1\% Pb (weight not given).

Find: ratio of concentration, recovery and theoretical head assay.

Definitions. Recovery is the percentage of the metal in the ore that reports to the concentrate. The theoretical head assay is the feed assay recalculated from the products: (metal in concentrate + metal in tailing) / weight of ore.

Step 1, ratio of concentration (weight of heads per unit weight of concentrate):

K = \frac{F}{C} = \frac{2000\ \mathrm{g}}{70\ \mathrm{g}} = 28.6

Step 2, lead in the products:

\begin{aligned} \text{Pb in concentrate} &= Cc = 70 \times 0.551 = 38.57\ \mathrm{g} \\ \text{Pb in head} &= Ff = 2000 \times 0.021 = 42.0\ \mathrm{g} \end{aligned}

Step 3, recovery (metal in concentrate over metal in ore):

R = \frac{Cc}{Ff}\times 100 = \frac{38.57}{42.0}\times 100 = 91.8\%

Step 4, theoretical head assay. The tailing weight is found by difference:

\begin{aligned} T &= F - C = 2000 - 70 = 1930\ \mathrm{g} \\ \text{Pb in tailing} &= Tt = 1930 \times 0.001 = 1.93\ \mathrm{g} \\ \text{head assay} &= \frac{Cc + Tt}{F}\times 100 = \frac{38.57 + 1.93}{2000}\times 100 = \frac{40.50}{2000}\times 100 = 2.025\%\ \mathrm{Pb} \end{aligned}

Step 5, check from assays only (two-product formula):

K = \frac{c - t}{f - t} = \frac{0.550}{0.020} = 27.5, \qquad R = \frac{c(f - t)}{f(c - t)}\times 100 = 95.4\%

The calculated head (2.025%) is below the assayed 2.1%; the gap comes from errors in sampling, weighing and assaying, and it is also why the weight-based and assay-based results differ.

Answer: ratio of concentration = 28.6 to 1; recovery = 91.8%; theoretical head assay = 2.03% Pb (against 2.1% assayed).

3b.html:
Screening sizes particles with a physical barrier: undersize falls through the apertures, oversize moves across the surface.

Purposes.

  1. Size control in comminution circuits: for minus ½ inch ball-mill feed, the roll product is screened at ½ inch; undersize goes to the mill, oversize returns to the rolls. This stops oversize passing on and avoids overgrinding.
  2. Scalping: bar screens ahead of coarse crushers remove material that is already fine enough, raising crusher capacity.
  3. Preparing sized feed for concentration (jigs, tables) and sizing final products to specification.

Factors affecting performance.

  1. Feed rate: a low feed rate and long screening time give almost complete separation, but high rates make a thick bed the fines must cross; high capacity and high efficiency are opposing, so a compromise is needed.
  2. Probability of hitting the screen matrix: only the open area passes particles, P = [(D_A - d)/(D_A + D_W)]^2 per presentation, so particles need many presentations; more open area raises it.
  3. Blinding: particles just larger than the aperture wedge in and block it; moving the screen (vertically and horizontally) frees them.
  4. Angle of approach and shape: perpendicular approach passes best; plate-like mica rides over the apertures.
  5. Nature of the feed: much near-mesh material lowers efficiency, as in closed circuit with crushers.
  6. Moisture: damp feed agglomerates and blinds; screen perfectly dry or wet, never damp. Wet screening is most efficient but needs dewatering.
pts: Purpose: size control in crushing and grinding circuits, for example the ½ inch roll product with oversize returned (closed circuit)
A further purpose: scalping before crushers, or sized feed for concentration, or product sizing
Feed rate: capacity and efficiency are opposing; high rates give a thick bed and lower efficiency
Probability of hitting the screen matrix and open area; particles need many presentations
Blinding by near-mesh particles, relieved by screen motion
Angle of approach and particle shape or orientation (mica rides over)
Nature of the feed: near-mesh material lowers efficiency
Moisture: damp feeds agglomerate and blind; screen dry or wet, never damp; wet screening most efficient but costly to dewater

3c.html:
Classification is a method of separating mineral particles of various sizes, shapes and specific gravities into two or more products on the basis of the velocity with which they fall through a fluid (usually water: wet classifying). Coarse, heavier and rounder grains settle faster than finer, lighter and more angular ones. It is used for particles too fine to be screened efficiently.

Principle.

  1. Terminal velocity. Gravity (less buoyancy) accelerates a particle, while the fluid resistance rises with velocity. When they balance, the particle reaches its terminal velocity and falls uniformly.
  2. Resistance. At low velocity it is viscous (shear); at high velocity turbulent (fluid displacement). In the viscous range Stokes' law applies:
v_t = \frac{d^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)\,g}{18\,\mu}

For equal density the larger particle falls faster; for equal size the denser one does.

  1. Sorting column. Fluid rises at a uniform velocity V: particles with v_t > V sink to the spigot, those with v_t < V go to the overflow.
  2. Size and density together. In water, 50 μm galena (7.5) settles with quartz (2.7) of about 98 μm.
  3. Free and hindered settling. Below about 15% solids particles settle freely and size dominates; in denser pulps the pulp acts as a heavy liquid and density gains weight.
pts: Defines classification: separation into two or more products by settling velocity in a fluid, which depends on size, specific gravity and shape
Coarse, heavy, round grains settle faster; used for particles too fine to screen
Gravity against resistance rising with velocity; at balance, terminal velocity and uniform fall
Viscous and turbulent resistance; Stokes' law or the rule that larger or denser particles settle faster
Sorting column (described or sketched): fluid rising at V; v_t > V to the spigot, v_t < V to the overflow
Size and density act together, for example equal-settling 50 μm galena and about 98 μm quartz
Free settling below about 15% solids (size dominant) against hindered settling in denser pulps (pulp acts as a heavy liquid, density gains weight)

4a.html:
Principle. When a mixture of magnetic and non-magnetic particles is carried across a magnetic field, the magnetic particles tend to stay in the field while the others pass through. The separator simply provides two paths: a gravitational path for the non-magnetic particles and a magnetic path for the magnetic ones.

Construction.

  • A rotating drum whose shell is non-magnetic (for example stainless steel), turning at a set speed.
  • Inside it, a stationary assembly of magnets (permanent or electromagnets) covering an arc of the drum on the feed side, with poles of alternating polarity (N, S, N, ...). As particles pass the alternating poles they turn over, which releases non-magnetic particles trapped among the magnetic ones.
  • A feed hopper or vibrating feeder above the drum, and a splitter below it dividing the tails bin from the magnetics bin.

Functioning.

  1. Dry feed falls in a thin, even layer onto the top of the rotating drum.
  2. As the particles reach the field, those with magnetic susceptibility are attracted toward the magnets but are stopped by the drum surface, so they are held on the shell and carried round with it.
  3. Non-magnetic particles feel no pull; gravity and the centrifugal force throw them off the drum on their normal trajectory into the tails bin.
  4. When the held particles pass the end of the magnet arc, the field vanishes and they drop (or are brushed off) on the far side of the splitter as mags.

Control and use. Field strength, drum speed (faster gives a cleaner but smaller magnetic product), feed rate and splitter position set the cut. Dry drums suit coarse feeds, up to about 120-150 mm; below about 6-8 mm wet separation is often better, because water stops magnetic and non-magnetic particles sticking together.

Construction: rotating non-magnetic drum around a stationary arc of magnets of alternating polarity

Magnetic particles are held on the shell, carried past the end of the magnets and released into the mags bin beyond the splitter

4b.html:
Frothers are heteropolar, surface-active organic reagents added in small amounts (50-300 g/t) to a flotation pulp to produce a stable froth. Examples: pine oil and cresylic acid.

Their molecules adsorb at the air-water interface, polar group in the water and hydrocarbon chain in the air, and lower the surface tension. This stabilises the bubbles so that they carry the hydrophobic mineral to the surface without bursting and hold it in a froth that is skimmed off. The froth must not be too stable to handle. Ideally frothers do not affect the mineral's floatability.
pts: Defines a frother as a surface-active reagent added in small quantity to produce a stable froth
Gives an example (pine oil, cresylic acid)
Adsorbs at the air-water interface and lowers the surface tension
Stabilises the bubbles so the mineral is carried to the surface and skimmed, without changing the mineral's floatability

4c.html:
The process. Air bubbles are passed through a pulp of fine mineral particles in water. Particles that water does not wet (hydrophobic) attach to the bubbles, rise and form a froth on the surface, which is skimmed off as the concentrate. Wetted (hydrophilic) particles stay in the pulp and leave as tailings.

Driving force. Attachment replaces a solid-liquid and a liquid-gas interface by a new solid-gas interface. It is stable only if the surface energy of the system falls. Per unit area:

\Delta G = \gamma_{sg} - (\gamma_{sl} + \gamma_{lg}) < 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \gamma_{sg} - \gamma_{sl} < \gamma_{lg}

With Young's equation at the three-phase contact, \gamma_{sg} = \gamma_{sl} + \gamma_{lg}\cos\theta, where \theta is the contact angle measured through the water:

\Delta G = \gamma_{lg}(\cos\theta - 1)

So a mineral with a larger contact angle attaches more strongly; when \theta \approx 0 the mineral is fully wetted and \Delta G \approx 0.

Why minerals differ. Breaking ionic or covalent bonds leaves charged surface sites that attract polar water molecules, so most minerals are hydrophilic. Solids held by van der Waals forces (sulphur, graphite, talc, molybdenite) leave uncharged surfaces and are naturally hydrophobic. Hence collectors are adsorbed to make the chosen mineral hydrophobic, and a frother keeps the bubbles and froth stable.

Limits. Only fairly fine particles float: if a particle is too large, its weight (and the fluid motion) exceeds the bubble-particle adhesion and the bubble drops its load.

Direct and reverse flotation. Normally the value mineral goes to the froth and the gangue stays in the pulp (direct flotation); in reverse flotation the gangue is floated.
pts: Describes the process: bubbles through a pulp, hydrophobic particles attach and rise into a froth that is skimmed; hydrophilic particles stay in the pulp
Driving force is the reduction of surface energy: a solid-gas interface replaces solid-liquid and liquid-gas, so attachment needs \gamma_{sg} - \gamma_{sl} < \gamma_{lg}
Contact angle with Young's equation, \Delta G = \gamma_{lg}(\cos\theta - 1), larger \theta means more hydrophobic
Links wettability to bonding: broken ionic or covalent bonds give charged, hydrophilic surfaces; van der Waals-bonded solids (the course book adds hydrogen-bonded ones) are hydrophobic
States that collectors impart hydrophobicity to the chosen mineral and a frother stabilises the froth
Only fine particles float, because a large particle's weight exceeds the adhesion to the bubble
Distinguishes direct flotation (mineral floated) from reverse flotation (gangue floated)

  • Being hydrophobic is necessary but not sufficient: fluid motion and particle mass also act against attachment, which is why the size range is limited.
  • The course book also calls hydrogen-bonded solids hydrophobic; that is doubtful, because a surface with broken hydrogen bonds hydrogen-bonds to water (ice and gypsum wet readily). The naturally floatable minerals are van der Waals solids such as graphite, sulphur, talc and molybdenite.
  • The paper prints "floatation"; the course uses both spellings for the same process.

5a.html:
A solid oxide film forms around the unreacted sulphide core (\mathrm{MS} + \tfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{SO_2}). \mathrm{O_2} must diffuse in and \mathrm{SO_2} out through it.

  1. The film grows thicker and its permeability to gases falls, so oxidation slows down.
  2. At the core \mathrm{O_2} falls and \mathrm{SO_2} rises, so the reaction tends to reverse.
  3. Some sulphur is held as sulphate at low temperature; heating harder risks sintering, which closes the pores.

So the last sulphur goes only slowly.
pts: An oxide film forms around the unreacted sulphide core as the particle is oxidised (\mathrm{MS} + \tfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{SO_2})
\mathrm{O_2} must diffuse in and \mathrm{SO_2} out through this layer; as it thickens its permeability falls and oxidation slows
Low \mathrm{O_2} and high \mathrm{SO_2} at the reaction front make the reaction slow down and tend to reverse
A further reason: sulphur held as sulphate at low temperature, or sintering at high temperature closes the pores

  • The key word is diffusion through the product layer; "the reaction is slow" without saying why earns little.
  • Remedies, if asked: fine grinding, rabbling or fluidising to expose fresh surface, excess air, and a longer time at temperature.

5b.html:
Definition. A predominance area (Kellogg) diagram is an isothermal plot, drawn from thermodynamic data, of \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} for a metal-sulphur-oxygen system, showing the area in which each condensed phase (metal, sulphide, oxide, sulphate) is stable.

Uses: it shows which product a given roaster gas and temperature give, so roasting conditions can be set for an oxide, a sulphate or a partial roast; superimposed diagrams of two metals show conditions for selective roasting.

Limitations: it gives equilibrium only (no rates); it assumes pure phases at unit activity (no solid solutions, mattes or ferrites); it holds for one temperature.
pts: Defines it as an isothermal \log p_{\mathrm{SO_2}} against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} diagram showing the stable condensed phase in each area, from thermodynamic data
A use: setting roasting conditions for the desired product, or selective roasting of two metals
Two limitations: equilibrium only (no kinetics), pure phases at unit activity, one temperature only

5c.html:
Construction. A typical multiple-hearth roaster has several (about 10) circular brick hearths superimposed on each other inside a cylindrical, brick-lined steel shell. A rotating central shaft, driven by a gear at the bottom, carries arms on each hearth, and mechanical rabbles (blades) on the arms move over the hearth surface. The shaft and arms are hollow, so air cools them. The drop holes alternate: at the centre of one hearth and at the periphery of the next.

How roasting is performed.

  1. The concentrate enters at the top hearth. The slowly revolving rabbles stir it and plough it towards the drop hole, so it drops from hearth to hearth in a zigzag path and is discharged at the bottom.
  2. Air enters at the bottom and flows upward, counter-current to the ore; the \mathrm{SO_2}-bearing gas leaves through the flue at the top.
  3. On a hearth only the particles at the surface meet the air, so rabbling keeps exposing fresh sulphide. While falling from one hearth to the next, each particle has its whole surface exposed and burns rapidly, so most of the roasting happens during the fall.
  4. The upper hearths dry and preheat the charge with the hot rising gas, the middle hearths roast it, and the lower ones finish it. Auxiliary burners are used when roasting is not autogenous or the charge is very moist.
  5. The temperature must stay below that causing fusion or sintering of the charge.
pts: About 10 circular brick hearths stacked inside a cylindrical brick-lined steel shell
Rotating central shaft with arms carrying rabbles over each hearth (hollow, air-cooled)
Ore fed at the top, ploughed by the rabbles to drop holes, falls hearth to hearth and is discharged at the bottom
Air enters at the bottom and rises counter-current; gases leave through the flue at the top
Only surface particles contact air on a hearth, so rabbling exposes fresh surface; most roasting occurs while particles fall between hearths
Upper hearths dry and preheat, auxiliary burners when not autogenous or moist; temperature kept below fusion or sintering
Neat sketch with shell and lining, hearths, central shaft with rabble arms, alternate central and peripheral drop holes, feed, discharge, air in and flue

  • Drop holes alternating at the centre and the periphery, with the zigzag ore path.
  • Ore feed at the top, calcine discharge at the bottom.
  • Air in at the bottom, flue gas out at the top.

5d.html:
Principle. A narrow molten zone is moved slowly along a partly purified solid bar, held in an inert container or atmosphere and melted by a ring heater. Impurities that lower the melting point collect in the liquid, travel with the zone to the far end, and that end is cut off.

From the phase diagram. The liquidus and the solidus both fall from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus more steeply, so at every temperature the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium with it:

k = \frac{C_S}{C_L} < 1

A melt of composition X (C_0) starts to freeze at L_1 and deposits solid S_1 with only kC_0.

Effect of the moving zone. Purer solid freezes at the back of the zone; the rejected impurity stays in the zone, which melts fresh charge at its front, so the impurity is carried forward. The first solid holds kC_0, the impurity content rises along the bar, and the last zone length freezes impure and is cropped.

Multiple passes in the same direction: the more passes, the purer the starting end. For k = 0.3 the start holds 0.3C_0 after one pass and about 0.01C_0 after five.

Conditions. k far from 1 and slow zone travel. Impurities with k > 1 move the other way, to the starting end. The method gives ultra-pure Si, Ge and Ga.
pts: Principle: a narrow molten zone moved slowly along a solid bar sweeps the impurities into the liquid and to one end, which is cut off
Phase diagram: temperature against impurity concentration, liquidus and solidus falling from T_m of the pure metal, three fields labelled, tie lines S_1L_1 and S_2L_2
States from the diagram that the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium, k = C_S/C_L < 1 (S_1 purer than L_1)
The purer solid freezes at the back of the zone and the rejected impurity is carried forward; the first solid holds kC_0 and the impure last part is cropped
Multiple passes in the same direction raise the purity at the starting end
A condition or use: k far from 1, slow zone travel, impurities with k > 1 move to the starting end, or products such as Si, Ge, Ga
5d.sketch:
• Axes: temperature (vertical) against impurity (solute) concentration (horizontal).
  • Liquidus and solidus both falling from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus below and steeper.
  • Fields labelled Liquid, Solid + Liquid, Solid.
  • Vertical line X for the melt C_0; tie line S_1 L_1 where freezing starts and S_2 L_2 where it ends.
  • k = C_S/C_L < 1 written on the diagram.
5d.watch:
• The phase diagram carries the marks for "principles": label the axes, both lines and the tie line, and say which composition is the solid.
  • Do not say the impurity "evaporates" or is "removed" in the zone: it is only redistributed along the bar, and the impure end must be cut off.
  • Fast zone travel lets the rejected impurity build up ahead of the freezing front, so the effective k moves towards 1 and each pass removes much less impurity.
  • Extra depth: silicon is refined by the floating-zone method (no container) because molten Si reacts with crucible materials and picks up oxygen and other contamination; after many passes the profile reaches a limiting (ultimate) distribution, set by k and the zone length.

6a.html:
Smelting and matte smelting

Smelting (reduction smelting) heats an ore, usually an oxide, with a flux and a reducing agent (coke) so that the oxide is reduced and the charge melts into liquid metal and an immiscible slag, with gases leaving:

\text{mineral} + \text{gangue} + \text{flux} + \text{reducing agent} \rightarrow \text{metal} + \text{slag} + \text{gas}, \qquad \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{CO}

Matte smelting fuses a sulphide concentrate (usually partly roasted) with a flux, without a reducing agent, to give a matte, a molten mixture of sulphides (\mathrm{Cu_2S} and FeS), under an immiscible slag; some sulphur leaves as \mathrm{SO_2}.

BasisSmeltingMatte smelting
Chargeoxide ore, flux, cokesulphide concentrate or calcine, siliceous flux
Chemistryreduction by C and COmainly melting; Fe partly oxidised and slagged
Atmospherereducingneutral to mildly oxidising
Productcrude metal (iron, lead)matte, an intermediate that must be converted
GasCO, \mathrm{CO_2}\mathrm{SO_2}

Extraction of copper by matte smelting

The process works because copper has a greater affinity for sulphur, and iron a greater affinity for oxygen: iron is oxidised and slagged, and copper stays as \mathrm{Cu_2S}.

  1. Concentration. Chalcopyrite (\mathrm{CuFeS_2}) ore with less than 2% Cu is upgraded by froth flotation to a concentrate of about 11 to 35% Cu.
  2. Partial roasting. Part of the FeS is oxidised; the reaction is not completed, so that no higher iron oxides form:
2\,\mathrm{CuFeS_2} + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + 2\,\mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad 2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}
  1. Matte smelting. The calcine is melted with quartz at 1200 to 1300 °C (reverberatory or flash furnace). Any copper oxide is turned back to sulphide, and FeO is slagged:
\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{FeS} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{FeO}, \qquad \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}

The denser matte collects below the slag; the slag is tapped off and discarded.

  1. Converting. Air is blown through the molten matte. Slag blow: FeS is oxidised and slagged, and the slag is poured off, leaving white metal (\mathrm{Cu_2S}):
2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}

Copper blow:

2\,\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\,\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}

The product is blister copper, about 99% Cu.

  1. Refining. Fire refining blows air to remove the dissolved sulphur ([\mathrm{S}] + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{SO_2}), then removes the dissolved oxygen with hydrocarbons (poling), for example \mathrm{CH_4} + 3\,[\mathrm{O}] = \mathrm{CO} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}; S falls from about 0.02 to 0.002% and O from 0.5 to 0.05%. The anodes are electrorefined to cathode copper of 99.99% Cu.
pts: Smelting: ore, flux and a reducing agent (coke) heated to give liquid metal, slag and gas, with a reduction such as \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{CO}
Matte smelting: sulphide charge fused with flux, no reducing agent, gives a matte (molten \mathrm{Cu_2S} + FeS) and an immiscible slag
At least two contrasts: metal against an intermediate that needs converting, reducing against neutral or oxidising conditions, oxide against sulphide feed, CO against \mathrm{SO_2}
Principle: Cu has the greater affinity for S and Fe for O, so Fe goes to slag and Cu to matte (or gives the sequence concentration, roasting, smelting, converting, refining)
Concentration of chalcopyrite (below 2% Cu) by froth flotation to about 11 to 35% Cu

Partial roasting with balanced reactions (2\mathrm{CuFeS_2} + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + 2\mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{SO_2}; 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2}), not taken to completion

Matte smelting with silica at 1200 to 1300 °C: \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}, and \mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{FeS} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{FeO} or "very little reaction, mainly melting"
Matte and slag immiscible; the denser matte settles below and the slag is removed
Converting, slag blow: 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and slagging with \mathrm{SiO_2}; slag poured off
Converting, copper blow: 2\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}, giving blister copper of about 99% Cu
Refining: fire refining (S oxidised by air, O removed by hydrocarbons or poling) and electrorefining to about 99.99% Cu

6b.html:
Given: 60 t of matte with 54% FeS; air with 21% \mathrm{O_2} by volume; \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2} slag; the copper blow ends with no excess \mathrm{Cu_2O} or \mathrm{Cu_2S}.

Find: (i) the volume of air to oxidise the FeS, (ii) the total volume of \mathrm{SO_2}, (iii) the mass of slag.

Assumptions: the rest of the matte (46%) is \mathrm{Cu_2S}; 1 t = 1000 kg; gas volumes at STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 22.4 \mathrm{m^3} per kmol. Molar masses: FeS 87.91, \mathrm{Cu_2S} 159.16, FeO 71.85, \mathrm{SiO_2} 60.09 kg/kmol.

Charge.

\begin{aligned} m_{\mathrm{FeS}} &= 0.54 \times 60\,000 = 32\,400\ \mathrm{kg} &\Rightarrow\ n_{\mathrm{FeS}} &= 32\,400/87.91 = 368.6\ \mathrm{kmol} \\ m_{\mathrm{Cu_2S}} &= 0.46 \times 60\,000 = 27\,600\ \mathrm{kg} &\Rightarrow\ n_{\mathrm{Cu_2S}} &= 27\,600/159.16 = 173.4\ \mathrm{kmol} \end{aligned}

(i) Air for the FeS (slag blow)

2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}
\begin{aligned} n_{\mathrm{O_2}} &= \tfrac{3}{2}(368.6) = 552.8\ \mathrm{kmol}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{O_2}} = 552.8 \times 22.4 = 12\,380\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ V_{\text{air}} &= \frac{12\,380}{0.21} = 58\,970\ \mathrm{m^3} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 5.90\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} of air at STP.

(ii) Total SO2

The copper blow oxidises part of the \mathrm{Cu_2S}, and the \mathrm{Cu_2O} then reacts with the rest:

\begin{aligned} 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} &= 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2} \\ 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} &= 6\,\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2} \\ \text{sum (divided by 3):}\quad \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{O_2} &= 2\,\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2} \end{aligned}

With nothing left over, one-third of the \mathrm{Cu_2S} is oxidised to \mathrm{Cu_2O}, and each kmol of \mathrm{Cu_2S} gives 1 kmol of \mathrm{SO_2}; each kmol of FeS also gives 1 kmol.

\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{SO_2}}(\mathrm{FeS}) &= 368.6 \times 22.4 = 8\,256\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ V_{\mathrm{SO_2}}(\mathrm{Cu_2S}) &= 173.4 \times 22.4 = 3\,884\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ V_{\mathrm{SO_2}} &= 8\,256 + 3\,884 = 12\,140\ \mathrm{m^3} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 1.21\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} of \mathrm{SO_2} at STP (542 kmol).

(iii) Slag

\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}\qquad (71.85 + 60.09 = 131.94\ \mathrm{kg/kmol})
\begin{aligned} m_{\mathrm{FeO}} &= 368.6 \times 71.85 = 26\,480\ \mathrm{kg}, \qquad m_{\mathrm{SiO_2}} = 368.6 \times 60.09 = 22\,150\ \mathrm{kg} \\ m_{\text{slag}} &= 368.6 \times 131.94 = 48\,630\ \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 48.6 t of \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2} slag.

(i) \mathrm{O_2} needed about 12,380 \mathrm{m^3} at STP (552.8 kmol)
(i) Air = V_{\mathrm{O_2}}/0.21 \approx 5.90\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} (58,900 to 59,000 \mathrm{m^3} with rounded masses)

(ii) Copper-blow reactions 2\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}, giving 1 \mathrm{SO_2} per \mathrm{Cu_2S}

(iii) Slag about 48.6 t (4.86\times10^{4} kg)

7a.html:
The two situations (sketches)

The reagent R must reach the mineral surface and the dissolved metal species M and products P must move away, across a liquid boundary layer.

(a) Complete dissolution. No solid product forms and the surface recedes (for example CuO in dilute \mathrm{H_2SO_4}). R falls from [R]_B in the bulk to [R]_S at the surface; M and P fall from [M]_S, [P]_S to their bulk values.

(b) Partial dissolution. The mineral decomposes and leaves a solid residue (for example \mathrm{CaWO_4} in carbonate solution leaves \mathrm{CaCO_3}). Leaching continues only if the residue is porous. I is the mineral/residue and II the residue/solution interface.

Kinetic steps

Case (a): (1) diffusion of R from the bulk to the surface; (2) reaction at the surface to a soluble metal species; (3) diffusion of M and P away into the bulk.

Case (b): (1) diffusion of R from the bulk to interface II; (2) diffusion of R through the porous layer; (3) reaction with the mineral at interface I; (4) outward diffusion of M and P through the layer; (5) diffusion of M and P from II into the bulk. The slowest step controls the rate.

Accelerating the leaching

  • Film diffusion (steps 1, 5) controlling: stir or agitate; the boundary layer thins and the rate rises until the layer reaches a limiting thickness.
  • Reaction (step 3) controlling: agitation has no effect; raise the temperature (activation energy 10-25 kcal/mol, 42-105 kJ/mol) and the reagent concentration.
  • In every case: finer grinding exposes more surface and shortens the path through any residue, which stirring cannot reach; higher temperature speeds up all steps, diffusion least.

Sketch (b): porous residue with interfaces I and II and the R, M, P profiles labelled

Case (b) five steps, including diffusion of R and of M, P through the porous layer and reaction at interface I
Film diffusion control: stirring or agitation thins the boundary layer and raises the rate up to a plateau
Reaction control: agitation has no effect; raise temperature (high activation energy, 10-25 kcal/mol) or reagent concentration
Finer grinding (more surface, shorter pore path) and higher temperature speed up leaching

7b.html:
Importance. A potential/pH (Pourbaix) diagram shows the stable species of a metal at each potential and pH, so it gives the pH (set by acid or alkali) and potential (set by an oxidant) at which the metal ion stays in solution. For example, Zn dissolves as \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} below pH about 6.9; Au needs cyanide.

Limitations.

  1. The sharp boundary lines are not absolute: one species merely predominates on each side.
  2. All major species must be included; omitting one can change the diagram dramatically.
  3. Equilibrium only: no information on rates, which need experiment.

7c.html:
Why purify

Leaching is rarely completely selective, so the pregnant liquor carries ions that interfere with later steps or contaminate the product. Purification removes them, or removes the desired metal selectively and leaves them behind (selective precipitation, ion exchange, solvent extraction).

Principle

Metal ions in solution exchange with specific ions held by a solid resin or a second liquid phase; the exchange is reversible and stoichiometric, so it removes unwanted ions or concentrates a selected one. The resin is an insoluble, chemically stable 3-D polymer framework of porous beads (0.5-1 mm); functional groups bonded to it supply the exchangeable ions and control the selectivity.

\begin{aligned} \text{cation exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{2\,R{-}SO_3H + Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons (R{-}SO_3)_2Cu + 2H^+}\\ \text{anion exchanger:}&\quad \mathrm{R^+Cl^- + A^- \rightleftharpoons R^+A^- + Cl^-} \end{aligned}

The cycle

  1. Loading: clear liquor flows through columns of resin, which takes up the metal ion; the barren solution is dumped.
  2. Elution: a small volume of strong solution reverses the reaction, giving a concentrated, pure eluate.
  3. Regeneration of the resin for the next cycle.

Example: uranium

\mathrm{H_2SO_4} leaching gives the complex anion \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}, while impurity metals are cations, so an anion resin takes only the uranium:

\begin{aligned} \text{loading:}&\quad \mathrm{[UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-} + 2R_2SO_4 \rightarrow R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 2SO_4^{2-}}\\ \text{elution (acidified chloride):}&\quad \mathrm{R_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 4Cl^- \rightarrow 4RCl + [UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-}}\\ \text{regeneration:}&\quad \mathrm{4RCl + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2R_2SO_4 + 4HCl} \end{aligned}

Plant and result

Columns A and B load in series while C is eluted; when A is saturated the columns change over, so the contact is counter-current. Impurities stay in the barren solution (purification); since both steps are nearly 100 % efficient, the metal is concentrated by about V_{\text{liquor}}/V_{\text{eluate}} (concentration).
pts: Need for purification: leaching is not selective, impurities interfere or contaminate; ion exchange is one of the methods

The cycle: loading, elution with a small volume of strong solution to a concentrated eluate, regeneration

8a.html:
Relative activity. The electrochemical series ranks metals by their standard reduction potential against the hydrogen electrode (0 V). The more negative E^\circ, the more reactive the metal and the harder its ion is to reduce: Au +1.50, Ag +0.80, Cu +0.34, H 0.00, Ni -0.25, Fe -0.44, Zn -0.76, Mn -1.18, Al -1.66, Mg -2.37, Na -2.71 V.

Cathode competition. In water the metal ion competes with hydrogen, and the reaction with the more positive deposition potential wins:

E_{\mathrm{M}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{M}} + \frac{0.0592}{z}\log a_{\mathrm{M^{z+}}} - \eta_{\mathrm{M}}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{H}} = -0.0592\,\mathrm{pH} - \eta_{\mathrm{H}}

The metal deposits when E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}}; \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is the hydrogen overvoltage on the cathode surface.

1. Metals nobler than hydrogen (Cu, Ag, Au). E_{\mathrm{M}} > E_{\mathrm{H}} even in strong acid and at low metal activity, so they deposit readily. Hydrogen appears mainly when the current density approaches the limiting current. Copper is won from about 150-180 g/L \mathrm{H_2SO_4} at 85-95 % current efficiency.

2. Less noble metals with a high hydrogen overvoltage (Zn, Cd, Pb, Sn, Mn). By equilibrium hydrogen should evolve first, but on these metals \eta_{\mathrm{H}} is about 0.7-1 V (against below 0.1 V on Pt), which pushes E_{\mathrm{H}} below E_{\mathrm{M}}. Zinc is won at 400-600 A/m^2, 35-40 ^\circC, on Al cathodes, at about 90 % efficiency, but only from a deeply purified electrolyte: Co, Ni, Sb, Ge lower \eta_{\mathrm{H}} and re-dissolve the zinc. Mn (-1.18 V) needs a near-neutral ammonium sulphate electrolyte and gives only about 60-70 %.

3. Less noble metals with a low hydrogen overvoltage (Fe, Ni, Co). They need a weakly acid (pH about 2-4), warm electrolyte, often with diaphragms, and give lower efficiency.

4. Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na, Ca, Li, Ti). E^\circ lies below about -1.6 V: no attainable overvoltage stops hydrogen evolution, the current goes to \mathrm{H_2}, and any metal formed reacts with water:

\mathrm{2Al + 6H_2O \rightarrow 2Al(OH)_3 + 3H_2}

Raising the pH does not help, because the hydroxide precipitates first.

Conclusion. Whether a metal can be electrowon from water is set by its potential relative to hydrogen, corrected for overvoltage, pH and concentration. The most reactive metals are won by fused-salt electrolysis: Al from cryolite-alumina, Mg from \mathrm{MgCl_2}, Na from NaCl.

Hydrogen overvoltage (high on Zn, Pb, Hg; low on Pt) moves the hydrogen potential below that of the metal, so Zn, Cd, Pb, Mn can deposit

Fe, Ni, Co with low overvoltage need pH control and give lower efficiency
Very reactive metals (Al, Mg, Na; E^\circ below about -1.6 V): hydrogen evolves instead and the metal would react with water (balanced equation)

8b.html:
Harmful impurities in electrical-grade copper

  1. Impurities that lower conductivity (in solid solution): P, Fe, Si, As, Sb, Sn, Ni, Co. Only 0.015-0.04 % P cuts the conductivity to about 85 % IACS, against about 101 % for electrolytic tough-pitch copper. Ag, Cd and Zn have little effect.
  2. Impurities that spoil drawing and annealing: Bi and Pb (grain-boundary films, hot shortness, wire breaks) and Se, Te, S (raise the softening temperature). Bi harms at a few ppm.

Elimination during electrorefining

Fire-refined anodes (about 99.5 % Cu) dissolve in a \mathrm{CuSO_4}-\mathrm{H_2SO_4} electrolyte at about 60 ^\circC and 0.3 V, and pure copper plates on the cathode:

\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-} \ \text{(anode)}, \qquad \mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu} \ \text{(cathode)}

The low cell voltage separates the impurities by potential:

  1. Nobler metals (Au, Ag, Pt metals) do not dissolve and fall into the anode slime; a little chloride precipitates dissolved Ag as AgCl.
  2. Se, Te (as \mathrm{Cu_2Se}, \mathrm{Cu_2Te}, \mathrm{Ag_2Se}), Pb (as \mathrm{PbSO_4}) and Sn (basic salt) are insoluble and go to the slime.
  3. Base metals (Ni, Fe, Zn, Co) dissolve and stay in the electrolyte, as their deposition potentials are far below that of Cu; a bleed stream removes them.
  4. As, Sb, Bi, close to Cu in potential, can co-deposit or form floating slime; the bleed and liberator cells keep them low.

Addition agents (glue, thiourea) and filtered electrolyte give a dense cathode of about 99.99 % Cu.

1. High electrical conductivity, so the voltage drop is small.
  2. Chemical stability in the electrolyte: not corroded, does not contaminate the product (a soluble anode dissolves evenly).
  3. Suitable overvoltage: low for the wanted reaction, high for unwanted ones (high hydrogen overvoltage on a zinc cathode).
  4. Mechanical strength, easy stripping of the deposit, low cost.
